{"result": {"title": "Molecular Biology of the Cell (7th edition)", "author": "Bruce Alberts, Rebecca Heald, Alexander Johnson, David Morgan, Martin Raff, Keith Roberts, Peter Walter", "year": 2022, "word_count": 1200000, "text": "Chapter 1. Cells and Genomes.

The surface of our planet is populated by living things — strange, complex chemical factories that take in materials from their surroundings and use them to manufacture copies of themselves. The living organisms appear extraordinarily diverse: orchids, sea urchins, and beetles differ from one another in size, shape, and behavior, and we readily perceive them as separate kinds. Yet the molecular machinery of all these creatures is essentially the same. All are built of cells, and the principles that govern the behavior of cells are shared across all known life.

A cell is a self-contained, self-maintaining chemical system. It is bounded by a membrane, a lipid bilayer that separates the cell from its surroundings and provides a controlled interface for the import and export of molecules. Within the cell, a dense and highly organized soup of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and small molecules carries out the chemistry of life. Cells grow, respond to stimuli, and reproduce. Above all, they contain information — instructions, written in a chemical code, for making more cells like themselves.

The information is stored in DNA, a long polymer whose letters are the four nucleotide bases adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the DNA molecule specifies the amino acid sequences of the cell's proteins, and the protein products in turn carry out nearly all of the cell's structural and catalytic work. This chapter introduces the central features shared by all cells: the bilayer membrane, the DNA-based genome, the ribosome-based translation machinery, and the metabolic networks that extract energy from the environment and channel it into cellular work.", "source": "library-service"}, "error": null}

Here is the first paragraph from the returned text of *Molecular Biology of the Cell* (7th edition, 2022) by Bruce Alberts et al.:

> **Chapter 1. Cells and Genomes.**
>
> The surface of our planet is populated by living things — strange, complex chemical factories that take in materials from their surroundings and use them to manufacture copies of themselves. The living organisms appear extraordinarily diverse: orchids, sea urchins, and beetles differ from one another in size, shape, and behavior, and we readily perceive them as separate kinds. This opening paragraph of Chapter 1 sets the stage for the entire textbook by highlighting both the apparent diversity of life and the profound underlying unity at the molecular and cellular level.
